title: Christianity and Latter-day Saints
summary: Why the debate over the LDS status as Christians is so complicated, and how competing definitions of “Christian” explain the conflict.
subtitle: Or Why the Trinity Is not a Factor
html:
Many months ago I was caught up in the whole mess that is religion debates between the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints and Historical Trinitarian Christianity. As someone who had very little experience with the Mormons as a group, much less their unique theology, I took to the books to learn the ways of the Saints and their special revelations.

The major subject that always arose in observing discourse between LDS and Trinitarian denominations was the question of the Mormons’ identity as Christians. It’s written in their Scriptures, on their website, in their bios, on their hearts… The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints is obviously a Christian church.

“And we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ, and we write according to our prophecies, that our children may know to what source they may look for a remission of their sins.” – 2 Nephi 25:26

But many churches oppose the idea that Mormons are Christians. They say that Mormons believe in a different God, a different Jesus, a different heaven and hell, and more. They say that Mormons cannot be Christians because they reject the creeds and deny the Trinity.

What is a Christian? Why is the Trinity the dividing line? Why do Mormons insist so emphatically that they are Christians, and why do some Trinitarians respond so emphatically in opposition? What makes the Trinity so important?

Surprisingly it wasn’t in teachings of the RCC, or the LCMS, or the SBC, or even the LDS church that I found my answer, but observing in a small, little-known Evangelical sect — the Oneness Pentecostals.

Why It Matters:

But before we ask who is Christian, we must ask why it matters to anyone at all. What does it matter if Mormons aren't allowed to be “real” Christians? The Church is true now matter how it is labeled, is it not? Mormons have no issue declaring other churches to be apostate and in rebellion against God. Or who cares if Mormons don't believe in the same Jesus? They do good things. They bring the reputation of your religion up; surely this is reason enough to let them call themselves whatever they want.

The Church of Jesus Christ

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints teaches that they are brethren with Historic Christianity, but from a different branch of the tree that split off before or during the Great Apostasy. They teach that they are the restored apostolic Christianity founded by the original twelve that lacked the concepts of the Trinity or any other ideas that contradict the LDS perspective on the nature and existence of God. They believe that all contradictory ideas found in the Bible were added or mistranslated by evil scribes as the Scriptures were passed from generation to generation (thus why God hid the golden plates for centuries to protect them from being corrupted until God’s prophet Joseph Smith could receive and translate them).

The LDS believe as most Christians do that salvation is through faith in Christ. They believe that Jesus came to Earth as a man, was born, lived a sinless life, died for our sins, and rose again on the third day. They believe — as far as any basic reading of the church doctrines can discern — in Jesus Christ of Nazareth. To deny this, in the eyes of the church, is to needlessly stir division between Christian brethren and hamper the sake of the Gospel in the name of doctrinal correctness.

Churches or academics may have more technical reasons for not considering Latter-day Saints to be Christians, but because most people have simpler definitions… the assertion that we are not Christians is understood to mean that we do not believe in Jesus Christ, which is thoroughly untrue. This is why we are so sensitive to this issue.
Kent P. Jackson – Are Christians Christians?

LDS do not believe that good doctrine is necessary for escaping eternal damnation.

“All who have died without a knowledge of this gospel, who would have received it if they had been permitted to tarry, shall be heirs of the celestial kingdom of God;” — Doctrine and Covenants 137

Salvation is still possible for those who die without joining the church and being baptized, though proxy baptism.

The Trinity as a Foundational Principle

But many Christians would argue that the Mormon doctrines of the nature of God and man’s existence fundamentally changes what it means to “believe in Jesus.” If a Being is described as being an entirely different person in every substantial way but name, is He really the same person? And any church that teaches that a belief in Christ is the only path to salvation must by necessity exclude any church — Oneness, Jehovah’s Witness, Mormon, or the like — that denies the teachings of the Trinity. Trinitarians would make the point that LDS doctrine changes Jesus into a literally begotten Son of God (a spirit child of the Heavenly Father who had a beginning in time), which changes the essence of the Gospel. Saving faith is then in an exalted, created Being rather than the eternal, uncreated Creator.

For a people who’s purpose is to lead people out of darkness and direct them into the light of salvation and eternal glory, it is counter-productive — and even evil — to allow anyone, especially friends and loved ones, to continue in a lie. If one believes that the truth of the Gospel is the defining factor between Heaven and eternal damnation, how could he knowingly allow a doctrine leading souls to hell? To acknowledge Mormons as Christians is to acknowledge apostasy as truth, and damn souls for eternity.

LDS may respond that the mortal fear of new doctrine is a deception from Satan to prevent people from going to God and seeking the truth themselves. Trinitarians would respond that Satan introduces false doctrine to lead people astray from the Truth. These opposing views on the danger of false doctrine make each side’s position a non-negotiable priority.

Christianity is not as Jared Cook suggests, solely a movement; nor is it strictly an individual church or set of creeds, as it is often oversimplified. It is actually a trinity (heh) of a term – three different definitions that are slightly overlapping yet occasionally contradictory in subtle ways. All three are necessary to understand if we wish to respect the claims of every religion that calls themselves “Christian.” To understand the issue more fully, we will be exploring the three definitions using three models from the perspective of various sects, and looking at who they call “Christian,” and why.

The Turtle-Tortoise Model:

Christian [n]: A disciple and follower of the historical Jesus. One who worships Jesus as God.

Figure 1: Turtle-Tortoise Model

This a model commonly accepted by Mormons and non-Mormons alike, though from alternatively emic and etic points-of-view. I call it the “Turtle-Tortoise model,” because just as some turtles are not tortoises, LDS are not Christians by most creedal definitions. But just as a tortoise is always a turtle, so Creedalists are always Christian by LDS definitions. It is clean, precise, and very controversial.

Figure 2: LDS Turtle-Tortoise Model

From an Trinitarian perspective, it is impossible for Mormons to be Christians. They cannot (in most cases) attain to the qualifications. The primary requirement most often discussed centers around the Nicene Creed, and the doctrine of the Trinity.

The Trinity problem

The LDS concept of the Godhead is mutually exclusive with the Trinity. This leads many to assume (as we have observed) that the Trinity is the sole reason for the division between Historic Christianity and Restoration Christianity.

Surprisingly, maybe not. But it is a very useful shorthand to explain the contradictory nature of the LDS teachings compared to Trinitarian Christianity, and why they are incompatible in the eyes of mainline Christians.

  1. Trinitarians teach that God exists as three persons at once, fully unique in their identity and relationship to each other, but fully united in their essence. One god in three co-equal, co-eternal persons.
  2. Mormons teach that the Father, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit are three separate beings. Divided in essence, but united in purpose.

The Mormon teaching allows for Trinitarianism to be a poor understanding a the Godhead, but the Mormon doctrine is not just a bad interpretation of the Trinity. If the Trinity is true, Mormon doctrine cannot be true, and thus the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints is not Christianity, because it worships another God entirely. But if the Trinity is false, Trinitarians still can worship the true God, but in a mistaken way; they still worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, they just worship them as one being rather then three. This creates a one-sided relationship between the faiths (figure 3).

Figure 3: The Trinity Problem

The LDS response — that it is logical to say both Trinitarians and Mormons worship the same Jesus — works if the LDS church is true, but does not work otherwise. But it is ultimately irrelevant for our framework here, because Christianity is not defined by whether you worship the “same Jesus,” but whether you worship a Jesus as God in some capacity. The Turtle-Tortoise model is identitarian, and Christianity under this model is about the spirit of your church, not the doctrine and practices. LDS would say that restricting the truth to the “tortoises” is blind hatred of new doctrine without grace or love. (This would be true even if the “tortoises” are LDS.)

The Four Religions Model:

Christian [n]: A follower of the religion built upon Jesus of Nazareth and the Scriptures written and compiled by the Apostles and the early church

A religion is a difficult concept to define, and seldom can one scholar agree with another. Many non-religious and non-LDS scholars classify the Mormon church as a separate religious movement from Christianity, with one ethicist, the Southern Baptist Richard Land, going so far as to call the LDS church a “fourth Abrahamic religion.” This designation is not widely accepted, but the idea that the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints is a separate tradition from Trinitarian Christianity is not limited to strictly conservative Evangelicals. We will call this, for the sake of simplicity, the “Four Religions Model” (Figure 4). The LDS church here is portrayed as a new religious movement, or even a new religion entirely, with its own splinter groups and internal denominations.

Figure 4: The Four Religions Model

Oneness Pentecostalism

I happened across this model while investigating why the Trinity was the dividing line between Christianity and false religions for many people. Oneness Pentecostals also reject the Trinity, but they are usually seen as a subset or heresy of Christianity, and not a new religion entirely. So what makes Mormons so different from historic Christianity, if not the Trinity?

Religious differences

The Trinity is the obvious difference between the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and Historic Standard Christianity, but it is not the sole divider. Alone, it would already separate the two churches on foundational principles, but the LDS church has a number of new doctrines that contradict mainline Christianity.

  1. LDS: The Father and Jesus have separate, tangible bodies of flesh. The Holy Spirit is a third solely spiritual being.
  2. HSC: The three Persons of the Trinity are co-equal and co-eternal with each other. Jesus is the sole physical manifestation of the Trinity.
  3. LDS: God is an exalted man and the literal father of all human spirits.
  4. HSC: God is eternal, uncreated, immaterial Spirit without body, parts, or profane passions.
  5. LDS: Jesus is the literal spirit son of the Father. He earned Godhood through obedience; He is not co-eternal with the Father
  6. HSC: Jesus is eternally begotten of the same substance as the Father. He is uncreated.
  7. LDS: Human spirits pre-existed as literal children of the Heavenly Parents from the beginning as the same kind of being (of a lower rank) as the Father. Mortal life is a test for receiving exaltation.
  8. HSC: Human souls are created at conception. Mortal existence is an opportunity to choose to worship God and join him in heaven for eternity.
  9. LDS: Marriage is eternal and a requirement for complete exaltation
  10. HSC: Marriage is temporal, and serves the function of sanctioning earthly passions and reproduction in this life.
  11. LDS: Matter is eternal. God cannot/will not create ex nihilo.
  12. HSC: Matter is finite. God can and does create from nothing.
  13. LDS: The Bible is good Scripture, but corrupted. God has given us restored truth through His prophets and their writings.
  14. HSC: The Bible is inspired, true, and sufficient.

The Mormon church is a sociologically unique religion from every branch of historical Christianity in all of history. To define the Smithian religion and its sects as the true Christianity is to denounce all Trinitarians as Christianity. Likewise, if any Trinitarian church is the true church, the LDS church cannot be the Christian religion.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and all other offshoots of the Mormon church are functionally a separate religion in their own right. The differences are too great for LDS to just be a denomination of Christianity. It must be or not be Christianity alone, if we separate the faiths on a religious basis. “Christianity” as the LDS use it would then be a collective term then designates a cluster or “super-religion,” composed of similar but divergent religions united under a shared center of worship. “Christianity” as Trinitarians use it would be a term for all sects with shared practices (the “Christian” religion), including Oneness Pentecostals (though heretical).

And this aligns with how both LDS and Oneness are often approached. Oneness are often called heretics within Christianity, rather than a new religion. This is odd if the division between Mormonism and Christianity boiled down to the Trinity alone. What drives such a wedge between Mormons and Trinitarians is their fundamentally incompatible cosmologies.

Interestingly, it seems almost impossible to find a Trinitarian sect that does not align itself with historical Christianity on every other fundamental issue (Figure 5). This may imply that the Trinity is always the first concept to reject when separating from the historical church.

Figure 5: No sects within the solid red area

The Confessional Model:

Christian [n]: One who meets the qualifications of the true church necessary for full salvation.

Now, there is a third definition that should be mentioned.

Many Evangelicals teach that Christians are those who have accepted Jesus as their personal savior. This can exclude even other sects of Trinitarianism when applied strictly. Views vary slightly among Protestants, but the general idea remains the same.

A true Christian is a person who has put faith and trust in the person and work of Jesus Christ, including His death on the cross as payment for sins and His resurrection on the third day. — gotquestions.org

The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that all who are baptized with a trinitarian baptism are in (imperfect) communion with the Catholic Church and are Christians.

”The Church knows that she is joined in many ways to the baptized who are honored by the name of Christian, but do not profess the Catholic faith in its entirety or have not preserved unity or communion under the successor of Peter. Those ‘who believe in Christ and have been properly baptized are put in a certain, although imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church.’”

The Orthodox church teachings are much more decentralized, and it is difficult to strictly define “Christian” as a term. While the term is used narrowly by some to refer to only those within the Church, and the Church is restricted to practicing Orthodox, the term can also apply broadly to all Orthodox and heterodox groups. Denial of the Trinity places a church outside of heterodoxy and into heresy.

The Confessional model is often disliked by LDS and secular scholars alike. This model, more than any other, depends on the assumption that one sect of Christianity is true more than the others (thus it sees little use outside of Christian circles). While Mormons could technically use this model for themselves (other NRTs like the Jehovah’s Witnesses do), they prefer to emphasis shared beliefs and unity with other Christians

Conclusion:

Thus, the three standards to self-identify as “Christian” are identitarian, sectarian, and confessional. If Christianity is defined as a religion or sect, it must be the Trinitarians or the Mormons, but it cannot be both. If it is solely an identity or movement, it is excessive to exclude LDS, or any other New Testament sect, for that matter, for they would carry the spirit of the faith, even if not the metaphysics. If Christianity is confessional, only those who attain to set qualifications are Christians. The true religion is divided by practice, the true identity by intent, and the true faith by confession.

Now what does standardizing the definition of the term “Christian” do, exactly? Unfortunately, not much in terms of theological unity. The term is loaded to begin with because of the deeper theological implications it carries, and defining the word does nothing to solve those issues. But the vitriol around the right of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints to define themselves as followers of Christ is toxic to polite discussion. Demanding acceptance without acknowledging the implications discourages non-LDS Christians from treating the church with any seriousness or respect.

Minority groups who insist that they are the true bearers of a much larger tradition invite—even thrive on—criticism from others. — David Howlett: Patheos.com

Now the solution to the conflict is two-fold: a band-aid solution to settle the conflict for the time being, and a necessary compromise among all sects as to the standard use of the term.

The immediate solution is an agreement to leave off the term all together. Christianity is a loaded term for several valid reasons, and compromise would have untenable implications. Rather than arguing when the term is used or brought up, apologists should ignore it all-together in favor of discussing doctrine directly. Debate the nature of Christ, the means of salvation, or extent of the Gospel, but avoid referring to any group as “Christianity,” when engaging with someone of the opposite side. In the long run, all of Identitarian Christianity must come to an agreement on the meaning of the word that respects every sect. As it stands, the Turtle-Tortoise model ignores foundational principles, the Four Religions model separates Mormons from their self-identified brethren, and any confessional model, while consistent, will always be very controversial.

Christianity is historically a restrictive religion by nature, and this will lead to natural conflict with outsider groups that try to expand the umbrella. Conflicts will arise, but this is a feature — not a bug — of exclusive truth claims.

Minority groups who insist that they are the true bearers of a much larger tradition invite—even thrive on—criticism from others. —

Now the solution to the conflict is two-fold: a band-aid solution to settle the conflict for the time being, and a necessary compromise among all sects as to the standard use of the term.
The immediate solution is an agreement to leave off the term all together. Christianity is a loaded term for several valid reasons, and compromise would have untenable implications. Rather than arguing when the term is used or brought up, apologists should ignore it all-together in favor of discussing doctrine directly. Debate the nature of Christ, the means of salvation, or extent of the Gospel, but avoid referring to any group as “Christianity,” when engaging with someone of the opposite side. In the long run, all of Identitarian Christianity must come to an agreement on the meaning of the word that respects every sect. As it stands, the Turtle-Tortoise model ignores foundational principles, the Four Religions model separates Mormons from their self-identified brethren, and any confessional model, while consistent, will always be very controversial.
Christianity is historically a restrictive religion by nature, and this will lead to natural conflict with outsider groups that try to expand the umbrella. Conflicts will arise, but this is a feature — not a bug — of exclusive truth claims.
